title: Into the market
hook: tenth picture: he walks into town with open hands, bringing gifts

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ninth picture: a river flowing, flowers simply red, the world seen as it was all along. Your line: just as it is. What ordinary thing did you let be exactly itself? Day one thousand two hundred thirty.

The last picture is noisy. After a silent circle and a quiet river, the herdsman is back, and he's walking into town. Barefoot. Chest bare. Smeared with dust and ash. A broad grin, and in some drawings a big belly too. He's carrying a gourd and a staff, and in some versions a sack over his shoulder. He's headed for the market, the wineshop, the crowd. No robe, no halo, nothing to mark him as anyone special. He's just a cheerful man among people, with his hands open. Today: into the market.
screen: `BAREFOOT, DUSTY, GRINNING.` → `A GOURD, A STAFF, OPEN HANDS.` → `HEADED FOR THE CROWD.`

segments.voice: First, the series doesn't end in a cave. It could have stopped at the empty circle, or the peaceful river. Instead it ends in a marketplace. The Chinese title of this picture says he enters the town with hands hanging down, an image of open, relaxed hands, ready to help. In this teaching, awakening that stays on the mountain isn't finished. It comes back down. Second, nobody can tell. The preface, in paraphrase, says his gate is shut and even the wise don't know him; his inner life can't be glimpsed. He doesn't seek out the footprints of the old masters. He doesn't need to look like a sage. He goes to the market with his gourd and comes home with his staff. Third, what he brings. The preface says he keeps company with drinkers and butchers, and they all become buddhas. The verse says he needs no secret art of the immortals, yet in front of him, withered trees come into bloom. That's a striking claim to end on, and it's carefully put. He doesn't preach. He doesn't recruit. He's simply among people, and things around him come alive. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day. In some paintings he looks like Budai, the laughing monk of Chinese folk tradition with his sack of gifts. Mahayana teaching holds up the bodhisattva, who seeks awakening for the sake of others, and this picture shows that help as ordinary company: buying vegetables, sharing a drink, listening to a neighbor. The whole long search, from the first footprint to the empty circle, comes out here, at a market stall, with open hands.
screen: `IT ENDS IN THE MARKET, NOT A CAVE.` · `NOBODY CAN TELL HE'S A SAGE.` · `WITHERED TREES COME INTO BLOOM.` · `AWAKENING AS ORDINARY COMPANY.` · then, large: `INTO THE MARKET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit and let the breath settle. Then let your hands rest open in your lap, palms up, relaxed, the way the herdsman walks into town. Bring to mind the places you'll go today: the store, the office, the group chat, the kitchen. Picture one person you'll likely meet there. Without making a plan, let one small way of helping them come to mind: a door held, a question asked, five minutes of real listening. Then rest with open hands. The bell holds the time.
Into the market. The tenth oxherding picture: the herdsman returns to town with open hands, ordinary and unnoticed, and the people around him come alive. Today's word.
Your line: into the market. Today, help one person in an ordinary place, without making it a lesson and without needing credit. Day one thousand two hundred thirty.

howItsDone: The oxherding series ends with the tenth picture, which some Zen teachers use to stress that practice returns to daily life and service; in Zen communities this shows up as work practice, care for others and ordinary kindness.

original.note: Chinese (ruchan chuishou): 'entering the market with hands hanging down', the name of the tenth oxherding picture.

trapdoor: what you thought: the last stage of awakening is leaving the world behind.
what it means: coming back to town, ordinary and unnoticed, with open hands to help.
what a scholar hears: the title's 'hanging hands' suggests relaxed readiness to help, and the verse joins it to withered trees blooming, with no secret art claimed.

notes: All oxherding material paraphrased. Check: preface (inside his gate even the wise do not know him; the beauty of his garden is hidden; no need to seek the footprints of the old masters; to the market with a gourd, home with a staff; everyone he looks at awakens) and verse (barefoot, chest bare, dusty; no magic to lengthen life; withered trees bloom). The preface's mention of wine is softened to 'gourd' and 'wineshop'; confirm.
Gloss of 垂手 ('hands hanging down') as relaxed readiness to help is a common reading; confirm.
'In some paintings he looks like Budai' and the sack 'in some versions': confirm.
'In Mahayana Buddhism, the point of awakening is to help others' is a broad statement of the bodhisattva ideal; Keeper to confirm wording.
Original 入鄽垂手; pronunciation approximates Mandarin ruchan chuishou.

Editor: hook's big belly now attributed to some drawings (the verse gives bare chest, bare feet, dust and ash); preface paraphrase corrected (drinkers and butchers become buddhas, not 'everyone he looks at'); verse now 'no secret art of the immortals' in voice, myth and trapdoor; cut 'that's no accident' and the sweeping Mahayana claim; reworded a line close to a modern translation.
